question: In April 2026, Italy’s National Ombudsman for the Rights of Persons Deprived of their Personal Freedoms presented its annual report for 2024 on developments in the areas under its remit, including the ‘various suitable facilities’ placed at the disposal of the Public Security Authority as a back-up (in the event that the specialised detention facilities are at capacity) for the temporary holding of non-EU nationals subject to a return decision.

The Ombudsman also highlighted other settings – such as border facilities and crossing points or reception centres for unaccompanied minors – where the de facto deprivation of liberty was a possibility, stressing that the lack of a formal framework governing such sites called for round-the-clock monitoring and stronger safeguards protecting fundamental rights.

In the absence of an up-to-date publicly accessible map locating these facilities and with only patchy information available on the way in which they operate and respect the legal rights of the detained, there is much concern about the ‘suitable premises’ and the detention conditions they offer.

Particularly in light of the new Return Regulation, can the Commission clarify whether it has any information on the suitable premises in the Member States, whether it intends to publish this information, and whether it deems these facilities and detention practices to be compatible with Union law?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.9.2026) The detention of third-country nationals for the purpose of return is currently governed by the Return Directive1, which lays down common standards and procedures for return and detention, including requirements concerning the grounds for detention, judicial oversight, detention conditions, and the protection of fundamental rights.

Under the EU legal framework, Member States are responsible for organising and managing detention facilities and for ensuring that any deprivation of liberty complies with EU law, including the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union2.

The Commission does not keep any inventory of all facilities that may be used by Member States for the temporary holding or detention of third-country nationals pending return. Consequently, the Commission is not in a position to provide such information.

The Commission monitors compliance with the Schengen acquis related to the return of thirdcountry nationals through the Schengen Evaluation and Monitoring Mechanism3. Italy’s last periodic Schengen evaluation took place in June and July 2021, including visits of preremoval detention facilities.

During a monitoring visit to some of these specialised detention facilities in April 2026, the evaluation team noted some improvements, while further efforts to improve detention conditions are still required.

1 Directive 2008/115/EC: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2008/115/oj/eng. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/treaty/char_2012/oj/eng. 3 Council Regulation (EU) 2022/922 of 9 June 2022 on the establishment and operation of an evaluation and
monitoring mechanism to verify the application of the Schengen acquis, and repealing Regulation (EU) 1053/2013, OJ L 160, 15.6.2022, pp. 1–27: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/922/oj/eng.
